opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The biggest shift for me has been moving from thinking of these models as inscrutable black boxes to seeing them as systems that do have real, discoverable structure inside, just not always the structure we'd expect.

When you actually intervene on a model's internals, swapping in activations from one input to another, or steering along a particular direction, you find that a lot of behavior is mediated by surprisingly localized and often fairly linear representations. A concept like sentiment, or whether a sentence is grammatical, or which entity a pronoun refers to, often lives in some identifiable subspace you can manipulate causally. That was not obvious a priori, and it's encouraging, because it means understanding isn't hopeless.

But I've also become more humble about what "understanding" means. Models are very good at finding solutions that are distributed, redundant, and context-dependent. You can find a circuit that explains a behavior on your carefully constructed dataset, and then it turns out the model uses a somewhat different mechanism on slightly different inputs. So I've come to think the right question isn't "what is *the* mechanism," but "what's a faithful abstraction of the computation at the level we care about, and how do we rigorously test that it's actually causal and not just correlational?"

The other lesson is that methods matter a lot. Some of the popular tools look compelling but, when you benchmark them honestly against simple baselines, like just prompting the model or training a basic linear probe, they don't always win. That's pushed me toward caring a lot about evaluation: if interpretability is going to be useful for controlling or auditing models, we have to show it actually works better than the cheap alternatives.

So overall I'm optimistic. There's real mechanism in there, it's often more human-legible than people feared, but we need to be careful and empirical rather than telling ourselves nice stories about what we find.

r001.rationale: The response says models have discoverable internal structure and that much behavior is mediated by identifiable representations and circuits.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the biggest thing interpretability has taught me is that these models are much more structured than the "giant inscrutable matrix" framing suggests, but structured in ways that don't map cleanly onto how we'd design a system ourselves.

When you actually go inside and look, you find features that correspond to recognizable concepts: a feature for a particular syntactic role, a feature for a specific entity, a feature that tracks whether we're inside a quotation. And you find circuits, little computational pathways where those features get combined to produce a behavior. That part is genuinely encouraging. It means the model isn't doing something fundamentally alien. It's doing something we can, in principle, write down.

But the second thing I've come to believe is that the organization is messy in a way that resists tidy stories. Features are superposed, so a single neuron or direction is often doing several jobs at once. The same behavior can be implemented redundantly by multiple pathways. And when you intervene, when you ablate a component or steer along a direction, the model often compensates in ways you didn't predict. So I've become skeptical of any interpretability result that claims "this is the mechanism" in the singular. Usually it's "this is one of the mechanisms, under these conditions, with this much of the behavior explained."

The third thing, and this is more of a methodological belief, is that causal intervention matters enormously. A lot of early work was correlational: you'd look at attention patterns or activation statistics and tell a plausible story. Those stories were frequently wrong. What's moved the field forward is being able to say, if I change this internal variable, the output changes in the way my hypothesis predicts. That's a much higher bar, and when a result clears it, I trust it a lot more.

So if I had to compress it: the mechanisms are real, they're discoverable, they're more distributed and redundant than you'd like, and you should only believe a claim about them if someone has actually gone in and poked.

r001.rationale: The response says features and circuits can produce behaviors and that mechanisms are discoverable, but it does not clearly claim that systematic mechanisms explain much of AI models’ behavior. It instead cautions that individual mechanisms explain only some behavior under specific conditions.

astra-6.text:
Interpretability has made me wary of assuming that a model solves a problem the way we would. We see a sensible answer and naturally imagine a sensible process behind it. But the same behavior can come from very different internal mechanisms—a general rule, a memorized association, or some shortcut we didn’t anticipate.

What’s encouraging is that those mechanisms aren’t completely beyond our reach. We can form hypotheses about what particular internal representations do, intervene on them, and see whether the model’s behavior changes. That gives us a stronger kind of evidence than asking the model to explain itself.

But I’d distinguish understanding a mechanism in a particular setting from understanding the model as a whole. Finding one circuit that contributes to an answer doesn’t mean we’ve found every way the model can produce that answer. So my takeaway is that there’s real structure we can uncover, but we should be careful about how far we generalize from each discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says internal mechanisms can differ and that a discovered circuit may contribute to an answer, but it does not clearly claim that systematic mechanisms explain much of a model’s behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest takeaway is that a model can learn useful internal structure without organizing it in a way that’s easy for us to understand. We tend to imagine a neat division of labor—this neuron represents one concept, that layer performs one operation—but the picture is often much more distributed. A single component can participate in several computations, and a concept can be represented across many components.

That also makes me cautious about explanations that sound too clean. If we find an activation that correlates with a behavior, that’s a clue, but it doesn’t establish the mechanism. The stronger test is whether intervening on it changes the behavior in the way our explanation predicts.

So I’d distinguish being able to describe what a model does from understanding how it does it. Interpretability is making progress on that second question, but finding one understandable mechanism doesn’t mean we’ve explained the whole model.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses investigating mechanisms and cautions that one mechanism does not explain the whole model, but does not express that systematic mechanisms can explain much of a model’s behavior.
